areas.acesso: Access control, distributed systems and names (ch.6-7)
areas.politicas: Policies, multilateral security, privacy and data (ch.9-11, 26)

itens.pergunta: Who are the likely opponents (spies, crooks, geeks, swamp), with what capability and motivation, and how does this change over the system's lifetime?
Does the threat model assume that spies' tools end up in criminals' hands (leaks)?
Does the attack scale (marginal cost per target falls)? Which targets fall to which vulnerability?
Were the supply chain and standards (components, libraries, vendors) considered as a vector?
Were competitors, suppliers and the organization's own executives considered possible opponents?
Is there a robust whistleblowing channel for internal reports, independent of HR?
Does the design consider abusability (several users per device, abusive partner, the buyer is not the only user)?
Does the scope of 'system' include people, usability and customers (sense 6 in the book) and not only technology?
Does the protection policy say WHAT is protected and FROM WHOM, avoiding protecting the wrong thing or the right thing in the wrong way?
Is there an incident response plan, enough logs to tell a botnet from a targeted attack, backups (ransomware) and payment procedures (BEC)?
Is the account recovery fallback (questions, e-mail, SMS) as strong as the primary authentication? The system is only as strong as its weakest fallback.
Is a bad-password list used instead of composition rules, and is forced periodic change avoided absent suspected compromise?
Are passwords stored with a random salt and a slow, strong one-way function?
Are there throttling and global rate control (not only per account), without opening a DoS through lockout?
Are default passwords (devices, service accounts, scripts) eliminated or forcibly changed?
Do failed-login logs avoid storing the passwords that were typed?
Do important accounts require a second factor, and was the fallback of that factor analyzed?
Is the easiest way to use the system also the most secure (secure defaults, painless updates)?
Does the communication flow with customers avoid training them to act insecurely (links in e-mails, requests by phone)?
Are data-subject requests (access, deletion) authenticated robustly?
Is the protocol's threat model realistic, and does the protocol address it? Which environment assumptions may change?
Is freshness ensured (random nonce or counter) with replay resistance, and were the trade-offs (memory vs resynchronization) assessed?
Does key diversification avoid shrinking the effective space (e.g. a 128-bit key derived from a 16-bit number)?
Do the challenges include explicit names (anti-reflection), and is the same key not reused across different applications?
Were revocation and dependence on synchronized clocks handled (Kerberos/TTP)?
Is the protocol a specialist/standard one, publicly reviewed (not designed in-house)?
Are formats unambiguous, and does the protocol avoid exposing the software that processes it to attack?
Practical test: can a third party buy a spare key, or is there a universal master key (BORA)?
Is an accredited, current library/toolkit used, with no home-made crypto or protocol?
Is the cipher mode authenticated (GCM/AEAD), are IVs/keys never repeated, and is ECB not used for long data?
Do hashes used against collisions have output >= 256 bits?
Is RSA used with randomized padding and current key sizes (>= 2048 bits)?
Is the source of randomness (RNG) trustworthy? (common factors, trivial certificates)
Was forward secrecy considered (transient keys)? Beware of unauthenticated middleperson attacks.
Is 'pluggable cryptography' avoided (risk in the negotiation protocol)?
FDE: does the password-derived key allow an offline attack? Is there a TPM/attempt limit?
For the use case, is ACL, capability, group or role the right mechanism? How is access revoked, and how is 'what can this user access' audited?
Are the principle of least privilege and secure defaults the basis of the architecture?
Was the isolation of containers/VMs/cloud IAM validated (containers share the kernel; excess permissions)?
Is memory safety (language, static analysis from the start, DEP/ASLR/CFI mitigations) in the plan?
Is every input treated as suspect (data interpreted as code, SQL injection)?
Were concurrency/TOCTTOU and stale data analyzed, and was the cost of propagating global revocation measured?
Are backup and fallback distinct and tested? Has restoration been rehearsed?
Does a forced outage (DoS) push the system into an insecure fallback?
Are identifiers/names unique, stable and with clear semantics (Needham's principles, Kent's law)?
Who pays when the system fails? Who decides? Who benefits from not seeing the problem?
Does the control serve the business or lock-in? Who is the 'attacker' of the mechanism (equipment owner, competitor)?
How to tell good products from bad (market for lemons)? Is there information asymmetry in purchasing?
Is the defense weakest-link, best-shot or sum-of-efforts? Is the investment aligned?
Is the control visible or effective (security theatre)?
Is there an agreed one-page security policy that the mechanisms can enforce?
Is MLS/Bell-LaPadula really necessary? Costs: label explosion, bloated TCB, covert channels.
Are information flows lateral (compartments, relationships) rather than hierarchical?
For health data: per-record ACL, notification, attribution, aggregation control (BMA)?
Is there a conflict of interest that requires a Chinese Wall (Brewer-Nash) and a cooling-off period?
'Anonymized data': who will try to re-identify it, with which side data? Would access control/consent be better?
If differential privacy is used: was epsilon decided as policy and the global budget defined?
Consent, security by default and transparency (defending their data is not the data subject's job)?
Are records append-only/immutable, with double entry and balancing as an alarm?
For each control: dual control or separation of duties? What is the prevent-detect-recover combination?
Who are the 30-40 trusted people? Are they minimized, well paid and watched?
Were employees asked 'if you wanted to commit fraud, how would you do it?'
Are there mandatory holidays/task rotation?
Does any business process defeat dual control (letter of guarantee, code over the phone, gateway)?
Key ceremonies with two truly separate components (different people)?
If the system must provide evidence: is there non-repudiation that withstands hostile experts?
Does nobody declare the system infallible (a prior probability of zero does not change with evidence)?
Is the physical threat model (Derek..Abdurrahman) explicit, and does the design not assume the wrong attacker?
Are alarm communications redundant and anonymous (against targeted DoS)?
Was the trade-off between missed alarms and false alarms handled (guards get tired)?
For seals: who inspects, with what FAR/FRR, is there 'gundecking', who forges materials, disposal?
Metering/tokens: controlled sales channel, counter safe against brown-out/lightning, date rollover?
Were FAR/FRR/EER measured on a large, diverse population (goats, lambs, wolves)?
Is the use 1:1 verification or 1:N identification? Was the birthday limit calculated?
Can the template be inverted (hill-climbing)? Do not treat it as a hash.
Is there a human operator and a fallback for the cases biometrics does not cover?
Trusted interface: what the user sees vs what the token signs? (A US$2000 HSM depends on the PC)
For tamper resistance: what is really worth protecting (physical token, counters, root of trust)?
Is there an accurate inventory for automated patching and network scanning?
Is the local network untrusted? Strong authentication between clients and servers?
Does spear phishing have technical mitigations (cloud attachments, filters, restricted devices), not only training?
IDS: was the base rate (false:real) and the cost of false alarms calculated?
PKI: public or private CA for your case (warrants, code signing)? Is CT monitored?
Mobile apps: is there revocation for stolen phones/former users (car rental)?
Does dependence on SMS/phone for authentication take SIM swap into account?
Is there a risk register with severity x probability, mitigation and a senior owner per risk?
Do hazards have >= 2 independent mitigation mechanisms (hazards x mechanisms matrix)?
Does threat modelling use 'meet in the middle' (system assets x attacker assets) and the six attack techniques?
Does the development cycle have security requirements, approved tools, static/dynamic analysis, fuzzing and a final review?
When fixing a vulnerability, was the toolchain updated to find similar ones?
Is there an IR plan with monitoring, repair, distribution and reassurance (CEO/board educated beforehand)?
Is there a coordinated disclosure policy and a channel for researchers?
Are errors declared openly (culture), and does the team own its code?
Does prioritization consider risk AND reward (not only 'tightening security')?
Are checklists/certifications not being used as false security (ISO 27001)?
Is the certifier paid by the party being evaluated? Is the certification a liability shield (Maximum Complacency)?
Was there hostile review (bug bounty, IV&V) and not only friendly review?
Is the test time consistent with the desired MTBF (k/t)?
If FOSS: how much effort did capable people spend, and do they say everything they find?
For how many years does the vendor fix the product? Is there a sustainability/patch plan over the lifecycle?
Are safety and security handled together (737 Max, medical devices)?
Can the training data be poisoned (user feedback)?
Does the classifier resist adversarial samples, and was the high-dimensional decision space considered?
Does the API/model allow extraction by querying or leakage of training data (memorized outliers)?
Were inputs that make the classifier slow (DoS) considered?
ML as IDS: are there complements (other sensors, a brittle mode that triggers 'I am under attack')?
Does the claim of ML for social prediction (performance, crime) have evidence beyond simple regression?
